findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Revenue Budget Monitoring for Quarter One (The Period to 30 June 2026)
findings.headline: £2.1m of the £10.7m savings programme (19%) is rated amber and at delivery risk
findings.detail: While 80% of savings are rated green (£8.6m), £2.1m remains amber with no red-rated savings yet. At-risk schemes include employee reductions (timing risk), procurement early payment scheme (implementation dependency), and Active Wirral strategy (delivery dependency). If these fail to land, the Q1 deficit widens from £3.8m to £5.9m.
findings.matters: The council's strategy to close the Q1 gap relies partly on delivering amber savings on time. Failure rates on amber schemes directly worsen the financial position and increase reliance on reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: £10.677m total approved savings, £8.607m green (80%), £2.070m amber (19%), £0.000m red
findings.quote: At Quarter 1, over 80% of the savings programme is assessed as deliverable. The remaining £2.070m is currently assessed as amber and will require continued management action.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Revenue Budget Monitoring for Quarter One (The Period to 30 June 2026)
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit forecast to remain around £60m despite potential government High Needs Stability Grant
findings.detail: DSG deficit was £66.4m at 31 March 2026 and is forecast to close 2026/27 at around £60m. While the High Needs Stability Grant could fund up to 90% if the council's SEND Reform Plan is approved, in-year demand continues to exceed available funding, causing the deficit to worsen. Treasury management costs related to DSG funding pressure are running at £0.605m.
findings.matters: Accumulated DSG deficits represent unfunded liabilities that require future borrowing or reserve drawdown. If government support is not approved or is less than expected, the council faces significant additional pressure.
findings.figures: £66.409m DSG deficit 31 March 2026, forecast £60m year-end 2026/27, £0.605m additional treasury pressure
findings.quote: However, even if approved, the deficit is currently forecast to rise back to around £60m by year-end because in-year High Needs demand continues to exceed available funding.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Revenue Budget Monitoring for Quarter One (The Period to 30 June 2026)
findings.headline: Council will rely on drawing reserves or using capital receipts if operational efficiencies do not materialise
findings.detail: The council explicitly states the Q1 deficit is manageable only through 'one-off backstop measures' including capital receipts, reallocation of earmarked reserves, delaying General Fund Balance contributions, or drawing balances. It warns these measures would 'reduce future financial resilience and weaken the Council's longer-term sustainability'.
findings.matters: Using reserves to close a current-year gap is a warning sign. It signals structural budget problems, not cash-flow timing, and it erodes the buffer available for future years or unexpected pressures.
findings.figures: £3.794m adverse variance, General Fund Balance £18.6m forecast (with planned £3.562m contribution at risk), available earmarked reserves £7.5m
findings.quote: The Quarter 1 forecast adverse position is manageable in-year; however, this would require reliance on one-off backstop measures that would reduce future financial resilience and weaken the Council's longer-term sustainability.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Revenue Budget Monitoring for Quarter One (The Period to 30 June 2026)
findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend is structural: prior-year £8.3m overspend exceeded all growth funding, and the problem is worsening
findings.detail: Despite budgeting £7.4m for identified 2025/26 pressures plus £10.4m for inflation and fee uplifts, the actual 2025/26 care overspend was £8.3m — exceeding total growth funding. This structural deficit has carried into 2026/27 with Q1 forecasting £4.8m adverse variance as placement volumes and complexity of need continue to rise faster than budgeted.
findings.matters: A lender must distinguish between timing issues and structural deficits. This is structural: the council built substantial growth for care inflation but it was insufficient, and the problem is accelerating, not stabilising.
findings.figures: £8.340m 2025/26 overspend, £7.400m budgeted growth, £10.370m inflation provision, £4.839m Q1 adverse variance
findings.quote: The final 2025/26 outturn included an £8.340m overspend in care budgets, which exceeded the level of growth built into the base budget. This means that existing demand and cost pressures have continued into 2026/27, with further placement activity and complexity creating additional pressure at Quarter 1.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Capital Outturn Report
findings.headline: Borrowing in 2025/26 creates £1.499m annual revenue charge from 2026/27, with MRP continuing for 50 years.
findings.detail: The £23.1m borrowed in 2025/26 creates a first Minimum Revenue Provision charge of £0.344m in 2026/27, plus £1.155m estimated interest, totalling £1.499m. Using the Annuity Method, MRP payments increase annually over 50 years, peaking in 2075/76 at £0.916m MRP alone. This represents a structural revenue commitment reducing budget flexibility.
findings.matters: Rising annual debt service erodes revenue budget headroom for service delivery. Long-term repayment obligations constrain the council's ability to respond to pressures or invest in new priorities, directly affecting creditworthiness.
findings.figures: 2026/27: £0.344m MRP + £1.155m interest = £1.499m; rising to £1.603m by 2031/32; MRP peaks in 2075/76 at £0.916m annually
findings.quote: This debt will be repaid via charges to the revenue budget over the lives of the assets created or enhanced (the maximum asset life the Council is permitted to use for this repayment is 50 years).

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Capital Outturn Report
findings.headline: Council identifies contractor insolvency as a real risk to scheme completion in current financial climate.
findings.detail: The document explicitly flags contractor insolvency as a material threat, stating that if it occurs, 'a decision will need to be taken regarding the future of the scheme.' This is presented not as a remote possibility but as an identified risk requiring contingency planning.
findings.matters: Contractor failures could halt schemes mid-delivery, stranding costs and delaying services. The council's identification of this as a likely scenario in the 'current financial climate' suggests elevated supply-chain risk in their capital program.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Similarly, should a contractor become insolvent in the current financial climate, a decision will need to be taken regarding the future of the scheme.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Capital Outturn Report
findings.headline: Material inflationary pressures on building materials are identified as risking scheme costs and deliverability.
findings.detail: The council reports that inflationary pressures create risk of cost increases on materials. Cost pressures identified that jeopardise delivery will require either additional funding or the scheme becoming 'no longer viable from a financial perspective.'
findings.matters: Inflation on in-progress schemes can force budget reallocation or cancellation. Schemes already in delivery face material cost risk, which could strain finances further and create stranded costs.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: Due to inflationary pressures within the economy, financial monitoring of schemes is of upmost importance to identify any potential budgetary issues that may arise such as an increase in the cost of building materials.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Capital Outturn Report
findings.headline: The council is actively reviewing capital schemes for financial viability and deliverability amid budget pressures.
findings.detail: The document states that schemes are being identified 'which may no longer be financially viable, essential, or deliverable.' The Corporate Change and Portfolio Board oversees this process, with the Change Advisory Board providing enhanced scrutiny of schemes encountering difficulties.
findings.matters: Budget-driven scheme cancellations reduce service improvements and growth capacity. This signals financial distress is now constraining strategic investment decisions, not just forcing deferrals.
findings.figures: Applies to £74.986m 2025/26 capital program
findings.quote: Given the budgetary pressures that the Council faces, a review of the Programme continues and identifies schemes with the directorates, which may no longer be financially viable, essential, or deliverable.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Capital Outturn Report
findings.headline: £17.08m in approved capital expenditure was re-profiled from 2025/26 to 2026/27.
findings.detail: The council deferred £17.08m in capital spending from 2025/26 to future years. While this reduced short-term borrowing costs, it indicates schemes are slipping delivery schedules. The council notes that re-profiling reduces borrowing costs but permanent savings only occur if schemes are abandoned; otherwise the full budget is required in future years.
findings.matters: Significant slippage raises questions about project delivery capability and scheme viability. Deferred spending means borrowing needs shift to later years rather than being avoided, compressing the council's debt trajectory.
findings.figures: £17.080m re-profiled to 2026/27
findings.quote: Note the additional year-end net re-profiling of £17.080 million from 2025/26 to 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Capital Outturn Report
findings.headline: Capital borrowing for 2025/26 reached £23.1m, a £2.636m increase from the Q3 forecast.
findings.detail: The council forecast £20.464m in borrowing at Q3, but final outturn was £23.1m—a 12.9% variance. This represents unplanned capital financing need in the final quarter, with associated additional revenue costs through Minimum Revenue Provision and interest charges.
findings.matters: Borrowing increases signal rising debt dependency and reduce future budget flexibility. Underforecasting suggests either weak planning or late-year pressures, both concerning to lenders managing credit risk.
findings.figures: £23.100m actual borrowing vs £20.464m Q3 forecast; variance £2.636m
findings.quote: The Council required borrowing of £23.100 million this year to finance the capital schemes covered by this report. This level of borrowing has increased from the forecast £20.464 million in the Quarter 3 Capital Monitoring Report.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Capital Outturn Report
findings.headline: Wirral received ministerial approval for £27.5m in exceptional financial support but did not draw the 2025/26 tranche.
findings.detail: In February 2025, the council received confirmation of a capitalisation direction of £20m in 2024/25 and £7.5m in 2025/26 to meet revenue costs through capital resources—a mechanism used only when councils cannot set a balanced budget. The council did not require the 2025/26 funding. EFS approval signals prior financial distress requiring government intervention.
findings.matters: EFS approval indicates a council was at severe financial risk; that the 2025/26 tranche was not drawn could mean either recovery or difficult decisions to avoid it. Either way, lenders assess whether this signals sustainable finances or masked problems.
findings.figures: £20.000m capitalisation direction 2024/25, £7.500m 2025/26
findings.quote: On 20 February 2025, the Council received confirmation that the Deputy Prime Minister was minded to approving a capitalisation direction of £20.000m in 2024/25 and £7.500m in 2025/26. However, this financial year it has not been necessary to call on this funding mechanism.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Significant governance and leadership turmoil in 2025/26 with acting then permanent CEO, new Council Leader, and shifting political settlement
findings.detail: The council experienced major changes to political and managerial leadership during 2025/26, including an acting Chief Executive followed by interim then permanent appointment of a new CEO. A new Council Leader was elected in May 2025. Additionally, significant changes to political settlement occurred with new Green Group leaders and formation of a Reform Group. This instability coincides with discovery of major governance failures and need to rebuild officer-member trust.
findings.matters: Leadership transition during a period of financial crisis and major governance failures raises questions about institutional stability and capacity to execute recovery plans.
findings.figures: N/A
findings.quote: There was a significant amount of change to political and managerial leadership in 2025/26. This included an acting Chief Executive, and the subsequent appointment of an interim and then permanent Chief Executive. A new Leader of the Council was also elected in May 2025.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Self-neglect cases in adult social care rose from 32 in 2023/24 to 81 in 2024/25 to 103 in 2025/26
findings.detail: Self-neglect cases among adults known to services have more than tripled in two years, rising from 32 in 2023/24 to 103 in 2025/26. The council notes that affected individuals often have multiple disadvantages including homelessness risk, addiction, and mental health issues. The council is developing new proposals for early intervention and prevention and considering wider system reviews.
findings.matters: Rising complexity and volume of adult social care cases, particularly self-neglect involving high-risk individuals, indicates growing demand pressures that will likely drive continued overspends in this budget area.
findings.figures: Self-neglect cases: 32 in 2023/24; 81 in 2024/25; 103 in 2025/26
findings.quote: The Wirral health and care system has faced growing complexity and neglect, with self-neglect cases rising from 32 in 2023/24, to 81 in 24/25, and 103 in 25/26.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Regeneration programme governance weaknesses and undisclosed financial risks require urgent assessment across portfolio
findings.detail: The council has identified deficiencies in its approach to regeneration, particularly in light of worsening financial conditions, reduced external funding, and diminished investor confidence. The council recognises the need to assess the financial risks and liabilities across the whole regeneration programme to ensure proper accounting in revenue, treasury management and capital plans. A Regeneration Review identified lack of clear vision, ineffective decision-making, and poor accountability.
findings.matters: The regeneration portfolio contains undisclosed financial exposures that need to be properly reflected in treasury management and could require additional borrowing or asset sales, impacting the council's financial position.
findings.figures: N/A
findings.quote: Assessing the financial risks and liabilities across the Council's whole regeneration programme to ensure that they are properly taken into account in revenue, treasury management and capital plans.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Capital Project Team faces challenges including poor project accounts, slow delivery of complex assets, and wrong team configuration
findings.detail: The council recognises that capital management capabilities have been dispersed and the Capital Project Team has faced multiple challenges. These include poor project accounts, slow progress in complex asset delivery, shifting customer requirements against limited financial resources, and overall poor management with the wrong team configuration. These issues were reported to Policy and Resources Committee in March 2026.
findings.matters: Systematic capital project delivery weaknesses mean future capital schemes (including schools work) are at elevated risk of cost overruns and governance failures like the Birkenhead scheme.
findings.figures: N/A
findings.quote: the Capital Project Team have faced a number of challenges in the delivery of their capital projects (this predominately includes schools capital work). This has included: poor project accounts, slow progress in the delivery of complex assets, shifting customer requirements/ expectations on what can be delivered with limited financial resources and overall poor management, alongside the wrong team configuration to be able to deliver this type of work with a modern approach that effectively manages client risk.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Property portfolio has 1,103 identified building issues with only 45% addressed, creating operational and cost pressures
findings.detail: Implementation of the Corporate Landlord Model and regulator inspection visits revealed a significant number of issues within the council's property portfolio. 1,103 actions relating to the physical state of buildings were identified, with only 45% addressed to date. The council notes that the volume of these issues is placing significant and additional resourcing pressures on the Asset Service. A new Director of Capital Programmes and Assets has been appointed to address this.
findings.matters: A large backlog of property maintenance issues consumes operational resources and creates liabilities, while the scale of required expenditure to address compliance and health & safety issues is not yet clear.
findings.figures: 1,103 actions identified; 45% addressed
findings.quote: 1,103 actions relating to the physical state of the Council's buildings were identified, with 45% of these addressed, focusing on the most pressing matters. This task is of particular importance, as the volume of these issues was placing significant and additional resourcing pressures on the Asset Service.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Adult and Children's Social Care spending continuing to drive budget overruns with no clear resolution mechanism in place
findings.detail: The council identifies sustained pressures in both Adult and Children's Social Care as the primary driver of the £7.3m 2025/26 overspend. The Council's budget for 2025/26 identifies total savings of more than £25m required, but savings delivery confidence is not clearly established. The council has commissioned CIPFA to undertake budget assurance work identifying areas where confidence levels were lower.
findings.matters: Social care cost pressures are not abating and savings plans have not been delivered, indicating the council may struggle to close the gap even with the planned £25m savings, requiring further government support.
findings.figures: 2025/26 overspend driven primarily by Adult and Children's Social Care; total savings of more than £25m required for 2025/26
findings.quote: the Council is currently forecasting a further £7.3m overspend for 2025/26, driven primarily by sustained pressures in both Adult and Children's Social Care

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Repeated in-year budget deficits requiring exceptional government support: £18.6m in 2024/25, £7.3m forecast for 2025/26
findings.detail: The council closed 2024/25 with an £18.6m overspend funded through Exceptional Financial Support (EFS). For 2025/26, it is forecasting a further £7.3m overspend driven primarily by Adult and Children's Social Care pressures. The council has applied for £6m additional EFS for 2026/27. Grant Thornton's audit report stated that the scale of financial challenges combined with low resources creates significant risk to financial sustainability.
findings.matters: The council is structurally unable to balance its budget and is becoming dependent on exceptional government support, indicating fundamental financial unsustainability and raising questions about borrowing costs and credit quality.
findings.figures: 2024/25: £18.6m overspend; 2025/26: £7.3m forecast overspend; £7.5m EFS approved in principle for 2025/26; £6m EFS requested for 2026/27
findings.quote: The 2024/25 financial year closed with an £18.6m overspend, funded through Exceptional Financial Support (EFS), and the Council is currently forecasting a further £7.3m overspend for 2025/26, driven primarily by sustained pressures in both Adult and Children's Social Care.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Birkenhead Town Centre Movement Scheme cost forecast rose from £11.9m (March 2024 award) to £24.3m (July 2025)
findings.detail: The scheme contract was awarded in March 2024 at £11.9m but forecast to cost £24.3m by July 2025. Internal audit found serious weaknesses in project governance, design assurance, and procurement processes. The contract was awarded with incomplete design work and inadequate site investigations, resulting in numerous compensation events. These governance failings represent a significant failure to meet principles of good governance.
findings.matters: A major capital scheme has more than doubled in cost due to poor governance and project management, indicating systemic weaknesses in how the council delivers infrastructure investment and manages contractor risk.
findings.figures: Contract awarded £11.9m in March 2024; forecast total cost £24.3m by July 2025
findings.quote: Internal Audit's review of the Birkenhead Town Centre Movement Scheme identified major weaknesses in project governance, design assurance, and procurement processes, leading to substantial financial and operational risks. The contract was awarded with incomplete design work and inadequate site investigations, resulting in numerous compensation events and escalating costs.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council holds £43.5m in LOBO loans with lender-controlled interest rate increase risk
findings.detail: £43.5m of the council's £472m debt consists of LOBO loans where the lender can force interest rate increases at set dates. The council must then either accept the new rate or repay early. This creates uncontrolled interest rate exposure.
findings.matters: If lenders exercise their options (likely if rates stay elevated), the council faces unexpected spikes in debt servicing costs or forced refinancing.
findings.figures: £43.5m LOBO exposure (9% of total borrowing). PWLB 10-year rates rose from 5.38% to 5.72% over the period.
findings.quote: The Council continues to hold £43.5 million of LOBO loans where the lender has the option to propose an increase in the interest rate at set dates, following which the Council has the option to either accept the new rate or to repay the loan at no additional cost.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Internal borrowing (using cash reserves instead of external debt) is temporary and approaching its limit
findings.detail: The council uses cash balances in lieu of external borrowing to defer costs. The report explicitly acknowledges this is temporary mitigation: as capital reserves deplete, the council will exhaust this option and be forced into external borrowing at market rates.
findings.matters: The council has limited financial optionality going forward and rising external borrowing costs are inevitable as reserves run dry.
findings.figures: Investments fluctuated between £27m and £60m during the year (31 March 2025: £33m; 31 March 2026: £52m), showing tight liquidity management.
findings.quote: The use of cash balances in lieu of borrowing is a temporary measure to delay incurring borrowing costs. Elements of the Capital Programme ultimately require funding via borrowing from external sources. As capital reserves are called upon, the resources temporarily available to use in lieu of external borrowing diminish, meaning the Council will reach a point when it is no longer possible to delay borrowing any further.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Short-term borrowing costs spiked to 5-7% at year-end, more than 50% above the year's average
findings.detail: The cost of temporary borrowing from other local authorities jumped significantly in the final quarter, reaching 5.0-7.0% against 4.0-4.5% for most of the year. This occurs against tightening in the inter-authority lending market driven by increased section 114 notices from other councils.
findings.matters: Market stress on short-term rates signals lenders view councils as higher risk. It constrains the council's ability to bridge cash timing gaps and forecasts higher refinancing costs ahead.
findings.figures: Short-term borrowing rates 4.0-4.5% for most of period; 5.0-7.0% at year-end. Base Rate fell from 4.5% to 3.75% over the year, yet short-term rates rose.
findings.quote: The cost of short-term borrowing from other local authorities has been similar to or a little above Base Rate for most of the period, with interest rates between 4.0% and 4.5%. However, as is commonly seen, rates rose higher towards the end of the financial year, with rates of 5.0% - 7.0% being seen.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Loan debt jumped £95m in one year to £472m, driven by growing DSG deficit
findings.detail: Council loan debt rose from £377m to £472m—a 25% increase in one year. The report names the growth in the DSG deficit as a main driver, alongside capital programme delivery. The DSG deficit is a structural statutory funding gap between grant and school spending that must be borrowed to cover.
findings.matters: Rapid debt growth driven by a structural shortfall in education funding signals ongoing pressure that cannot be deferred and will persist across financial years.
findings.figures: Loan debt £472m at 31 March 2026 vs £377m at 31 March 2025 (£95m increase). DSG deficit is explicitly named as a main driver.
findings.quote: The level of loan debt held on the balance sheet was £472 million at 31 March 2026. This is an increase of £95 million since 31 March 2025. The main drivers for this increase being the growth in the DSG deficit position and the continued delivery of the capital programme.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Treasury management produced a £1.8m budget overspend in 2025-26 due to rising debt costs
findings.detail: Net treasury activities resulted in a budget overspend of £1.8m for the year. Debt management costs grew faster than investment returns could offset. This position was incorporated into the Revenue Outturn report.
findings.matters: It shows the cost of debt is accelerating and investment income is insufficient to cover it, pressuring the revenue budget.
findings.figures: £1.8m overspend on net treasury activities; investment income £2.2m actual (budgeted £1.7m but down from £2.4m in 2024/25)
findings.quote: Treasury Management had a budget overspend of £1.8m in the 2025/26 financial year on net treasury activities.

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 Revenue Outturn
findings.headline: Treasury management costs rose £2.44m due to increased reliance on Exceptional Financial Support and growing Dedicated Schools Grant deficit
findings.detail: Treasury management costs reported an adverse variance of £2.44m (9%), driven by increased costs associated with higher Exceptional Financial Support borrowing and the accumulating Dedicated Schools Grant deficit which requires debt servicing.
findings.matters: This represents structural growth in the council's debt servicing costs. The DSG deficit is compounding and requires long-term revenue provision.
findings.figures: £2.44m adverse variance (9% of budget); increased EFS reliance; growing DSG deficit
findings.quote: Rising treasury management costs are being driven by increased reliance on Exceptional Financial Support and the growing Dedicated Schools Grant deficit.

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 Revenue Outturn
findings.headline: Business rates collection rate fell 126 basis points year-on-year to 93.75%, amid economic uncertainty and retail relief changes
findings.detail: Business rates collection fell from 95.01% to 93.75%. The council attributes this partly to a climate of economic uncertainty, changes to retail/hospitality/leisure relief (reduced from 75% to 40%), and delays in rateable value changes by the Valuation Office Agency.
findings.matters: A 126bp decline signals economic stress in the borough and represents increased cash flow risk. If this trend continues, it reduces financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Business Rates collection 93.75% (2024/25: 95.01%); Council Tax 93.19% (2024/25: 93.74%)
findings.quote: The collection rate of 93.75% in 2025/26 was achieved despite a climate of economic uncertainty, changes to retail Hospitality & Leisure Relief down to 40%, previously 75% in 2024/25

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 Revenue Outturn
findings.headline: Housing Benefit subsidy losses are a £3m recurring pressure the council explicitly expects to increase year-on-year
findings.detail: The 2025/26 outturn reports a £3m adverse variance on Housing Benefit subsidy loss due to insufficient government subsidy for temporary and supported accommodation. The paper notes these costs are 'increasing year on year' and the council is 'driving through a number of initiatives to mitigate the losses', suggesting no sustainable solution has been found.
findings.matters: This is unfunded demand-led pressure that will recur and grow. If homelessness/temporary accommodation demand continues to rise, this becomes a structural budget gap.
findings.figures: £3m adverse variance; costs rising annually with insufficient subsidy
findings.quote: The costs of Housing Benefit Subsidy loss are increasing year on year and the Council is driving through a number of initiatives to mitigate the losses.

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 Revenue Outturn
findings.headline: The £4m contingency budget was fully consumed in year, leaving no buffer for 2026/27 pressures
findings.detail: The council allocated approximately £4m contingency during budget-setting and deployed all of it to offset adverse financial movements across the year. This contingency sits in the Strategic Holding Account and has been entirely utilised.
findings.matters: Any new unbudgeted pressure in 2026/27 will immediately require directorate cuts or reserve drawdown; there is no residual flexibility.
findings.figures: £4m contingency fully utilised
findings.quote: the Council allocated approximately £4 million in contingency funds during the budget-setting process. These funds are held within this area to help offset any adverse financial movements and have been fully utilised in year

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 Revenue Outturn
findings.headline: The council deferred £3.062m of planned General Fund Balance contributions to achieve a nominal balanced position
findings.detail: Of £3.562m planned contribution to General Fund Balance, only £0.5m was made; £3.062m was deferred. The final General Fund Balance stands at £14.980m, representing approximately 3% of the 2026/27 net revenue budget. This is the minimum prudent level for a council managing rising social care demand.
findings.matters: This leaves minimal buffer for unexpected pressures or delivery shortfalls in 2026/27. With £7.4m new social care funding and unmet asset sales targets, any adverse variance will immediately threaten reserves.
findings.figures: £3.062m deferred; only £0.5m contribution made of £3.562m planned; General Fund Balance £14.980m (3% of budget)
findings.quote: Delaying £3.062m of the planned contribution to General Fund Balances

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 Revenue Outturn
findings.headline: The council fell £4.1m short on savings targets, with asset sales programme delivering only 15% of planned £0.75m Estate Transformation savings
findings.detail: Delivered £21.313m of £25.446m approved savings (84%). Estate Transformation and Corporate Landlord Model achieved only £0.1m of £0.75m target; the Hamilton and Conway building sales have been pushed beyond 2025–26 due to planning delays, moving revenue savings into 2027/28. Active Wirral Strategy £1m saving slipped due to outsourcing delays and consultation timelines.
findings.matters: Suggests directorate savings assumptions are not robust; the council is becoming dependent on one-off corporate items and contingency drawdowns rather than structural efficiencies.
findings.figures: £4.133m undelivered savings; £0.75m Estate Transformation target vs £0.1m achieved; £1m Active Wirral slippage; Libraries 8-site model saving £0.175m abandoned
findings.quote: The timing means they are unlikely to be delivered until 2027/28. Achieving best value for the sale price will delay the point at which revenue savings can be realised.

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 Revenue Outturn
findings.headline: Adult social care costs surged despite stable placement numbers, driving £9.8m directorate overspend
findings.detail: Adult Care & Health reported £9.788m adverse variance (6% of budget). The overspend was not driven by increased volume—placement numbers in residential, nursing and domiciliary care remained broadly stable—but by rising per-unit costs due to increased complexity of individual care packages and the growing proportion requiring one-to-one support. An additional £7.4m has been added to base budgets for 2026/27.
findings.matters: This represents a structural cost increase that will not diminish with volume controls. If complexity continues to drive costs faster than funding, it creates a recurring gap.
findings.figures: £9.788m adverse variance; additional £7.4m in 2026/27 base budget; Older People Services £2.761m overspend; Mental Health & Disability £5.581m overspend
findings.quote: The overspend in residential care is not being driven by an increase in the number of placements, but by the higher cost of placements and the increasing complexity of individuals' needs.

findings.paper_title: 2026-33 Capital Programme
findings.headline: Interest rate exposure on £61.787m borrowing unhedged; estimates £1.069m–£2.780m annually
findings.detail: Interest cost estimates are acknowledged as indicative only, subject to market conditions and cashflow timing when borrowing occurs. Estimates show £1.069m in 2026/27 rising to £2.780m by 2028/33. The risk section identifies interest rate increases as a key risk, with officers assessing options to fix rates but no commitment yet made.
findings.matters: Unhedged interest exposure on large borrowing could materially worsen revenue position; lenders need clarity on rate management strategy.
findings.quote: Interest costs are estimated, based on a forecast average rate of borrowing for the period covered in Table 5. This is for indicative purposes only, the actual rate of borrowing will be determined by cashflow requirements and market conditions at that time.

findings.paper_title: 2026-33 Capital Programme
findings.headline: Total MRP payments rising to £12.746m by 2029/30, combining historic and new borrowing
findings.detail: Total Minimum Revenue Provision (principal repayment of capital debt) rises from £9.232m in 2026/27 to £12.746m by 2029/30. This includes both historic borrowing and new £61.787m from the current programme. The new borrowing alone adds £0.830m–£1.130m annually to revenue, creating decades of structural debt service pressure.
findings.matters: Rising MRP constrains revenue budgets and reduces flexibility; a lender must monitor whether debt service remains sustainable.
findings.figures: Total MRP 2026/27: £9.232m; 2029/30: £12.746m; new borrowing adds £0.830m–£1.130m annually
findings.quote: It is estimated that these MRP costs will peak in 2076/77 at £2.338 million reflecting the fact that the principal repayment associated with debt (the MRP) increases over the expected life of the asset funded from borrowing.

findings.paper_title: 2026-33 Capital Programme
findings.headline: Council accepts only capital bids that self-finance, address vital health/safety needs, or are strategically critical
findings.detail: The council explicitly states severe financial circumstances with no surplus revenue budget. Only bids that self-finance their capital costs, address vital health/safety needs, or are strategically critical can progress. This gatekeeping reveals tight financial position and limited headroom.
findings.matters: This constraint indicates financial stress and limited ability to respond to emerging priorities.
findings.figures: No new discretionary bids accepted without revenue offset
findings.quote: With no surplus revenue budget readily available to finance new bids, only bids which can self-finance the associated capital financing costs and/or are vital to Health and Safety or strategically important can be considered for inclusion.

findings.paper_title: 2026-33 Capital Programme
findings.headline: Capital Receipts Reserve depleted to £0.079 million, limiting financial flexibility
findings.detail: The council's available capital receipts balance (after ring-fenced reserves) is critically low. Future receipts are projected at £5.517m (2025/26), £7.260m (2026/27), and £2.940m (2027/28) but are explicitly acknowledged as uncertain due to economic factors. The council relies heavily on asset disposals to fund capital investment.
findings.matters: Low reserves constrain the council's ability to respond to unexpected needs and increase reliance on borrowing.
findings.figures: £0.079m available at 1 April 2025; projected receipts £5.517m–£7.260m–£2.940m
findings.quote: The available balance for general use in the Capital Receipts Reserve at 1 April 2025 was approximately £0.079 million.

findings.paper_title: 2026-33 Capital Programme
findings.headline: Council requires £61.787 million of borrowing to fund the 2026-30 capital programme
findings.detail: If delivered as forecast, this capital programme will require significant borrowing over 2026/27 to 2029/30, creating debt repayment obligations lasting decades. Revenue costs alone are £3.193m in 2027/28 (£0.830m MRP plus £2.363m interest), and MRP peaks at £2.338m annually in 2076/77.
findings.matters: A lender must assess the council's borrowing appetite and debt service capacity; finance directors face decades of revenue commitments.
findings.figures: £61.787m borrowing; 2027/28 revenue cost £3.193m; 2026/27 interest £1.069m; MRP peaks 2076/77 at £2.338m
findings.quote: If the Capital Programme is delivered as forecast in this report (with borrowing required over the period 2026/27 to 2029/30), the Council will require borrowing of £61.787 million to finance the capital schemes.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 BUDGET AND MEDIUM-TERM FINANCIAL STRATEGY
findings.headline: Staffing reductions signaled: council will 'shrink overall in terms of established posts' with potential collective redundancy notices.
findings.detail: Section 151 officer states budget will 'require the organisation to shrink overall in terms of the number of established posts and a reorganisation of how some services are provided'. Council working through voluntary exits and vacant post deletions but flags potential Section 188 notices (collective consultation for 20+ redundancies in 30 days) or HR1 forms. Trade unions want to avoid compulsory redundancies, but council notes 'the possibility of needing to serve these documents cannot be ruled out'.
findings.matters: Formal redundancy notices are visible sign of financial distress and workforce contraction. Carry legal and reputational risk. Fact that council is keeping this possibility on table indicates magnitude of spending challenge.
findings.figures: Undefined scale; potential Section 188 notices if 20+ compulsory redundancies in 30 days
findings.quote: It will require the organisation to shrink overall in terms of the number of established posts and a reorganisation of how some services are provided

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 BUDGET AND MEDIUM-TERM FINANCIAL STRATEGY
findings.headline: Council Tax at maximum referendum threshold; every 1% shortfall requires £1.9m additional savings.
findings.detail: Proposing maximum Council Tax increase (4.99%: 2.99% core + 2% Adult Social Care precept) before referendum required. Section 151 officer notes every 1% reduction creates £1.9m budget gap requiring additional savings. Council Tax already at maximum legal extent and provides zero flexibility for further increases without triggering referendum.
findings.matters: Council Tax is most politically controllable funding lever and is already maxed out. Removes option for closing future gaps and puts full pressure on spending control and government support.
findings.figures: Council Tax increase 4.99% (maximum before referendum); every 1% change = £1.9m swing in budget gap
findings.quote: This is the maximum allowable increase before a Council Tax referendum is required. Every 1% change in council tax assumptions increases or decreases the budget gap by approximately £1.9m in 2026/27

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 BUDGET AND MEDIUM-TERM FINANCIAL STRATEGY
findings.headline: Transformation savings will not close 2026/27 gap and full benefits will take years to realize.
findings.detail: Council identified six strategic transformation themes (customer journey redesign, commissioning, estate, service models) but acknowledges 'the full benefits will take time to materialise and will not close the 2026/27 budget gap'. Identified £10.7m of savings plus £4.6m financial improvements (including Council Tax Support changes) totalling £15.3m, but insufficient to close underlying gap.
findings.matters: Transformation programmes notoriously underperform. Council's acknowledgment that transformation will not solve 2026/27 problem is admission that near-term structural deficit exists and requires continued EFS or further policy changes.
findings.figures: £10.7m savings identified + £4.6m financial improvements = £15.3m total; £6m EFS still required
findings.quote: the full benefits will take time to materialise and will not close the 2026/27 budget gap

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 BUDGET AND MEDIUM-TERM FINANCIAL STRATEGY
findings.headline: Medium-term projections show £5.3m deficit in 2027/28 and £1.1m in 2028/29, with explicit Section 114 risk warning.
findings.detail: Government funding (excluding Council Tax) projected to reduce £5.3m in 2027/28 and £1.1m in 2028/29. Section 151 officer states this 'render the position untenable without decisive action' and warns that 'without sustained external support and transformation delivered at scale and pace, the Council will be unable to absorb rising statutory demand within diminishing core resources, eroding reserves and significantly elevating Section 114 risk'—explicit warning about inability to set a balanced budget.
findings.matters: Council signaling that even with transformation and savings, it may face structural deficit requiring further exceptional support or statutory intervention. Not a one-year problem; embedded in funding landscape and demand pressures over MTFP period.
findings.figures: £5.3m reduction in government funding 2027/28; £1.1m reduction 2028/29
findings.quote: the projected reductions in Government funding of £5.3m in 2027/28 and £1.1m in 2028/29 render the position untenable without decisive action. Without sustained external support and transformation delivered at scale and pace, the Council will be unable to absorb rising statutory demand within diminishing core resources, eroding reserves and significantly elevating Section 114 risk

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 BUDGET AND MEDIUM-TERM FINANCIAL STRATEGY
findings.headline: External debt exceeds Capital Financing Requirement—a Prudential Code breach.
findings.detail: Council's external borrowing projected to exceed CFR (the allowable borrowing limit for capital) by end of 2025/26 and expected to remain above CFR at end of 2026/27. Statutory guidance requires debt below CFR except temporarily. High Needs Stability Grant will reduce DSG deficit by ~£55m but insufficient to bring debt back below CFR. DSG cumulative deficit forecast at £104.9m by end 2026/27.
findings.matters: Breach of Prudential Code compliance (even temporary) signals financial stress and limits future borrowing flexibility. Indicates magnitude of SEND/DSG crisis—a national policy failure being carried by council. Rising debt servicing costs constrain future revenue budgets.
findings.figures: DSG cumulative deficit £104.9m by end 2026/27; external debt projected to exceed CFR at end 2026/27; High Needs Stability Grant ~£55m (Autumn 2026)
findings.quote: the Council's level of external borrowing is projected to exceed its Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) by the end of 2025/26. External debt is expected to remain above the CFR at the end of 2026/27

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 BUDGET AND MEDIUM-TERM FINANCIAL STRATEGY
findings.headline: Children's Assisted Travel Service demand out of control: 13% increase in one year despite £3.3m top-up.
findings.detail: Demand surged 13% in 2025/26 vs 2024/25. Despite injecting £3.3m additional funding, the service still forecast to overspend by £2m. Council responded with policy changes (agreed January 2026) to mitigate future demand growth, but scale of overspend suggests demand is outpacing intervention capacity.
findings.matters: Service experiencing double-digit demand growth that absorbs budget top-ups but still overruns signals demand assumptions are broken or delivery inefficient. This is a statutory service (school transport), limiting cut options. Pressure will recur unless underlying drivers change.
findings.figures: 13% demand increase in 2025/26 vs 2024/25; £3.3m additional funding injected; £2m overspend still forecast
findings.quote: In 2025/26, demand for this service increased by 13% compared with 2024/25. Despite an additional £3.3 million being built into the 2025/26 budget, the service is still forecasting an overspend of £2 million

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 BUDGET AND MEDIUM-TERM FINANCIAL STRATEGY
findings.headline: Adult Social Care demand spiking: 1,000+ more clients in two years with rising complexity.
findings.detail: Council notes 'over 1,000 more people are receiving support compared to two years ago and complexity is growing'. Budget includes substantial rebasing to align resources with current demand, inflationary pressures (6.7% Real Living Wage increase), and demographic growth. Policy change to Minimum Income Guarantee expected to generate £2.2m annual savings.
findings.matters: Demand-led services rising faster than policy interventions can offset represent structural budget risk. If demand continues to grow, savings from policy changes will be consumed by volume growth, creating recurring deficits.
findings.figures: 1,000+ additional service users in two years; Real Living Wage increase 6.7%; MIG savings £2.2m annually (£0.7m in 2026/27)
findings.quote: over 1,000 more people are receiving support compared to two years ago and complexity is growing among older adults, individuals with disabilities, and those with mental health needs

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 BUDGET AND MEDIUM-TERM FINANCIAL STRATEGY
findings.headline: General Fund reserves at 3.6% of net budget, below prudent 5% target, with recovery planned by 2029/30
findings.detail: Reserves have been 'critically depleted over time through ongoing efforts to mitigate budgetary overspends', leaving 'limited resources to fund crucial transformation initiatives'. External auditor recommended accelerating reserve-building. Current planned balance £18.042m (3.6% of budget); target 5% by 2029/30—a multi-year recovery.
findings.matters: Low reserves severely constrain ability to handle unforeseen pressures or demand spikes. This reduces financial resilience and increases risk that future pressures force service cuts or further EFS dependence.
findings.figures: Current General Fund balance 3.6% of net revenue budget; target 5% by 2029/30; planned balance £18.042m in 2026/27
findings.quote: The Council's current level of reserves and balances is low and does not provide sufficient capacity to address the existing budget gap or to safeguard against unforeseen financial risks. Reserve levels have been critically depleted over time

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 BUDGET AND MEDIUM-TERM FINANCIAL STRATEGY
findings.headline: Budget balances only with £6m of Exceptional Financial Support debt, not funding.
findings.detail: The council cannot close its budget gap through savings alone. It is relying on £6m of EFS (a capitalisation direction, which is borrowing) to set a balanced budget. The Section 151 officer states this 'is not sustainable and must be addressed'. EFS introduces ongoing debt servicing costs that constrain financial resilience.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that the council's apparent balance is contingent on securing government support which adds debt servicing costs and reveals underlying structural deficit. The officer's own warning that this is unsustainable is material.
findings.figures: £6m EFS required in 2026/27; revenue budget £495.222m
findings.quote: the 2026/27 budget is capable of being balanced; however, this is contingent upon securing agreement of £6 million of Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) from the Government

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 – Audit Findings Report for Wirral Council 2024/25
findings.headline: Material overall adjustments of £202.3m to Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement, with net increase to usable reserves of only £1.357m
findings.detail: The auditor identified numerous adjustments totalling £202.3m to the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement during the course of the audit. Despite this large figure, the overall impact on usable reserves (the council's liquid financial resources) was only a £1.357m increase, indicating that many adjustments offset each other or affected non-cash items.
findings.matters: The disparity between large adjustments (£202.3m) and minimal impact on usable reserves (£1.357m) suggests the council's draft financial statements contained significant errors across multiple areas. This pattern indicates inadequate financial reporting controls and raises questions about the reliability of the council's interim reporting.
findings.figures: £202.3m total adjustments to CIES, £1.357m net increase to usable reserves
findings.quote: We have identified a number of adjustments to the financial statements that have resulted in a £202.3m adjustment to the Authority's Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement. The overall impact on the level of the Authority's usable reserves is an increase of £1.357m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 – Audit Findings Report for Wirral Council 2024/25
findings.headline: IFRS 16 leases implementation added £124.23m lease liabilities and £50.42m right-of-use assets to balance sheet, plus £28.87m PFI liability increase
findings.detail: First-year implementation of IFRS 16 required recognition of operating leases on the balance sheet. Wirral recognised £124.23m in lease liabilities and £50.42m in right-of-use assets. Additionally, PFI liabilities were restated to reflect indexation of unitary payments since scheme inception, adding £28.87m to opening liabilities. These are accounting policy changes, not economic deterioration.
findings.matters: The £124m new lease liabilities represent a material increase in the council's obligations and reduce borrowing headroom under any debt covenants. Lenders need to understand whether existing loan covenants (such as debt-to-revenue ratios) are affected by these technical accounting changes.
findings.figures: £124.23m lease liabilities, £50.42m right-of-use assets, £28.87m PFI liability increase on transition
findings.quote: The implementation of IFRS 16 has resulted in a year-end balance of £124.23m Lease Liabilities and £50.42m Right of Use Assets being recognised on the Balance Sheet... This has resulted in in a £28.87m increase of the opening liability as of 1 April 2024.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 – Audit Findings Report for Wirral Council 2024/25
findings.headline: Revenue recognition control deficiency: invoices approved by staff not on authorised signatory list
findings.detail: During audit testing of revenue controls, auditors identified instances where invoices were requested and approved by individuals not included on the authorised signatory list, indicating the revenue approval process was not being consistently followed. While extended testing did not identify improper recognition, the control weakness exists.
findings.matters: This control gap creates risk of income overstatement, which is a known pressure point given the auditor's explicit identification that fees, charges and other service income could be overstated to achieve balanced accounts given financial pressures.
findings.figures: Control deficiency identified in revenue process; no material misstatement detected in testing
findings.quote: we identified a control deficiency whereby in certain instances invoices were requested and approved by individuals not included on the authorised signatory list. This demonstrates that the process for raising and approving invoices was not being consistently followed.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 – Audit Findings Report for Wirral Council 2024/25
findings.headline: Land and buildings fixed asset register errors totalling £11.422m identified through audit completeness check
findings.detail: Auditor testing identified numerous classification and accuracy issues in the fixed asset register affecting Land and Buildings valuations with a cumulative impact of £11.422m. The auditor has recommended improvements to processes for maintaining a complete and up-to-date fixed asset register, indicating systematic control weaknesses.
findings.matters: Fixed asset register errors of £11.4m indicate the council does not reliably track its asset base. This matters for loan covenants tied to asset values and for understanding the council's true property holdings and their condition.
findings.figures: £11.422m cumulative impact on Land & Buildings balance
findings.quote: Our completeness check of the fixed asset register and revaluations accounting treatment identified numerous classification and accuracy issues with a cumulative impact on Land & Buildings balance of £11.422m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 – Audit Findings Report for Wirral Council 2024/25
findings.headline: Birkenhead Commercial District regeneration scheme: £76.6m lease liability incorrectly omitted from prior year accounts, followed by £69.1m impairment in current year
findings.detail: The BCD finance leases that commenced in a prior year were not properly accounted for initially. Once corrected, the scheme resulted in £76.6m lease liability, £32.8m leased building asset and £43.8m leased asset under construction. In 2024/25, the auditor challenged management on indicators of impairment and accounting treatment, resulting in a £69.1m impairment charge being recognised on the leased assets.
findings.matters: The BCD scheme represents a significant capital commitment with both prior-year accounting failures and current-year massive impairment. For lenders, this demonstrates a troubled commercial development with deteriorating value and inadequate financial controls over major capital schemes.
findings.figures: £76.6m lease liability, £32.8m leased building asset, £43.8m leased asset under construction, £69.1m impairment, £13.2m net reduction in asset value
findings.quote: Contained within the lease liabilities figure is £76.6m which relates to the Birkenhead Commercial District (BCD) regeneration scheme finance leases which had commenced in prior year and were not appropriately accounted for... resulted in £69.1m impairment being recognised on the regeneration scheme leased assets

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 – Audit Findings Report for Wirral Council 2024/25
findings.headline: Pension asset accounting error corrected with £65.27m prior period and £177.669m current year adjustment
findings.detail: The council had incorrectly recognised a net pension asset without applying the asset ceiling as required by IFRIC 14. This resulted in a £65.27m prior period adjustment and a £177.669m current year adjustment to correct the error. The overall usable reserves increased by only £1.357m despite £202.3m of total adjustments, indicating this and other adjustments significantly reduced the council's position.
findings.matters: A £177m accounting correction on the pension liability demonstrates material accounting control weaknesses. For a lender assessing the council's net assets and borrowing capacity, this error materially affects the balance sheet and raises questions about financial statement reliability.
findings.figures: £65.27m prior period adjustment, £177.669m current year adjustment, £33.088m pension liability at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: The Council had recognised a net pension asset without applying the asset ceiling as required by IFRIC 14 resulting in a £65.27m prior period adjustment and £177.669m current year adjustment.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 – Audit Findings Report for Wirral Council 2024/25
findings.headline: Auditor identified significant weaknesses across all three value-for-money criteria and issued statutory recommendations
findings.detail: Grant Thornton concluded that Wirral has not made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources. The auditor has issued statutory recommendations under Section 24 and Schedule 7 of the Local Audit and Accountability Act 2014 relating to these weaknesses, which cover financial sustainability, governance, and improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness.
findings.matters: Statutory VFM recommendations represent a formal finding that the council's financial management is inadequate. Lenders need to know the auditor lacks confidence in the council's governance and sustainability.
findings.figures: Three criteria for VFM: financial sustainability, governance, and improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness
findings.quote: We identified significant weaknesses in the Authority's arrangements across all three criteria of financial sustainability, governance and improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness and so are not satisfied that the Authority has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources.

findings.detail: The report states that if the committee does not engage with the review findings, there will be risks to reputation and credibility with external organisations including external audit. This implies the review has identified material findings that require action.

findings.headline: Staffing retention identified as a key challenge for regeneration delivery
findings.detail: The council explicitly flags that retaining and attracting staff to its regeneration function will be an important focus. This is a capability concern that directly affects delivery of regeneration ambitions.
findings.matters: Loss of experienced staff in regeneration risks slippage or failure of capital schemes and economic development initiatives. Staffing instability in a strategic function is a delivery risk lenders assess.

findings.detail: Wirral commissioned Aughton Lane Limited to review the council's regeneration approach and assess the status of current regeneration projects. The review was completed over summer 2025. The council is now asking the committee to agree the findings and commit to an action plan by 31 December 2025.

news_drafts.headline: Wirral awarded up to £27.5m exceptional financial support for 2024/25 and 2025/26, and asks again for 2026/27
news_drafts.lead:
Wirral Council was awarded up to £27.5m of exceptional financial support (EFS, government permission to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending) for 2024/25 and 2025/26, according to its external auditor's annual report for 2024/25, which went to the Audit and Risk Management Committee on 27 October 2026.

The auditor's report says the council could not balance its 2024/25 budget without government intervention. It used up to £20m of EFS that year, of which it utilised £18.6m. The report says this is the second time the council has been awarded EFS since 2021.

The council has since asked for EFS for the financial year 2026/27. A review by the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy (CIPFA) was commissioned by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government following that request. The committee paper says the review was commissioned as a condition associated with the EFS and has no direct additional financial implications. It was carried out in April and May 2026.

news_drafts.headline: Wirral schools funding deficit forecast to reach £120m by end of 2026/27, funded by borrowing
news_drafts.lead:
Wirral Council expects its schools funding deficit to reach £120m by the end of 2026/27 and is paying for it by borrowing. The figure is in the council's prudential indicators (the limits and measures every council must publish to show its borrowing is affordable), which go to full Council on 12 October. The deficit is an overspend on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, mainly on support for children with special educational needs.

The papers say the council is meeting the deficit through capital borrowing rather than from its day-to-day budget, and describe it as continuing to grow. As a result, its borrowing is above its capital financing requirement (CFR), the total it has spent on long-lived assets and not yet paid for, in effect its underlying need to borrow. At 31 March 2026 borrowing was £640.335m against a requirement of £565.087m. By 31 March 2029 it is estimated at £744.893m against £582.922m.

The government has announced a High Needs Stability Grant, payable in autumn 2026, equal to 90% of the deficit at the end of 2025/26, which stood at £66.410m. High needs is the part of school funding for children with special needs. The council says the grant "will not be sufficient to bring the Council's external debt back below its CFR", and expects borrowing to remain above the requirement at the end of 2026/27.

news_drafts.headline: Merseyside Pension Fund audit unqualified pending £13.6m investment variance resolution
news_drafts.lead: Grant Thornton's audit of the Merseyside Pension Fund is anticipated to result in an unqualified opinion on its financial statements, subject to completion of outstanding work. However, auditors have identified a £13.6m difference between the fund's valuations of complex investments, known as Level 3 assets, and confirmations from external managers as at 31 March 2026. The fund's accounts, with net assets of £12,189m, do not adjust for this variance. Management asserts the difference is immaterial both quantitatively and qualitatively, sitting above the £7.3m reporting threshold but below performance materiality of £109.5m. Auditors are still awaiting three Level 3 investment confirmations from fund managers and one related party declaration before finalising their opinion. The audit fee is proposed at £128,262.
